campaign.title: Plane change
campaign.briefing: Reach a circular orbit at {orbit}, inclined 64-66° to the equator, from Cape Canaveral on a Soyuz. Range safety stops the Cape from launching steeper than about 60°, so the last few degrees have to be turned after launch. You can steer some of the inclination in the ascent, and turn the rest in orbit; you can launch straight to {orbit}, or launch lower and climb. Each choice moves the bill between the launcher and the upper stage. Which combination is cheapest?

launchSites.reason: its corridor reaches 64-66° directly, so there is no plane change to make; the mission is about the Cape corridor’s 60° limit

campaign.title: Geostationary
campaign.briefing: Climb from a low parking orbit to geostationary orbit: {geo}, circular, within 1° of the equator, held for three revolutions, on an Ariane 5. Its hydrogen upper stage burns at the equator crossing to raise apogee; separate it there, and your satellite circularises and removes the launch-site inclination together at apogee, where the plane change is cheapest. A site near the equator pays twice: more of Earth’s rotation in the ascent, less plane to remove.

launchSites.reason: its corridor’s lowest inclination is about 56°: removing that at apogee costs more than the Ariane’s upper stage and the satellite carry together

campaign.title: Escape
campaign.briefing: Leave Earth for good with at least 3 km/s to spare (hyperbolic excess speed). The Soyuz upper stage gives you a strong first kick; after it separates, your own stage pushes only 5 kN, and one long burn would spend its thrust far from perigee. Split the rest over several perigee passes, raising apogee each time, so every burn happens deep in Earth’s gravity where it counts most.

campaign.title: Lunar flyby
campaign.briefing: Fly past the Moon at {pass} without hitting it, on a Falcon 9. Launch when your site passes under the Moon’s orbital plane (from a site too far from the equator to reach that plane, into a plane through where the Moon will be), so one prograde burn of the upper stage in the parking orbit does the job; the burn’s timing sets where you meet the Moon. Launch steeply or high and the upper stage runs short: your probe has to finish the burn.

campaign.title: Free return
campaign.briefing: One injection, no corrections: swing around the Moon and fall back into Earth’s atmosphere below 11.5 km/s, as Apollo’s free-return trajectories did. The budget covers the ascent and the injection only, and a minute’s change in its timing misses the return corridor.

campaign.title: Lunar orbit
campaign.briefing: Enter orbit around the Moon (periselene {peri}, aposelene below {apo}) and stay for three revolutions. Ariane’s hydrogen upper stage is efficient but weak: the injection takes about ten minutes, so centre it on the right point and aim for a low pass. Then separate it; your spacecraft brakes at periselene.

campaign.title: Venus flyby
campaign.briefing: Fly past Venus ({pass}) in the spring 2028 window on an Atlas V. Pick a departure date from the porkchop plot, then a launch site, time and azimuth whose parking orbit contains the departure direction: it lies 35° north of the equator, so the parking orbit must be inclined at least that much, which costs the ascent some of Earth’s rotation. The Centaur has just enough for the departure if you launch well; your probe’s small engine can make up only a little.

campaign.title: Mars flyby
campaign.briefing: Fly past Mars ({pass}) in the 2028-29 window on a Falcon 9. Its upper stage can just make the departure from a low parking orbit launched close to due east; a higher orbit or a steeper launch leaves it short, and your probe carries only about 800 m/s for the difference and the corrections.

campaign.title: Mars orbit
campaign.briefing: Capture into an elliptical orbit around Mars (periapsis {peri}, apoapsis {apo}) and hold it for two revolutions. The Falcon 9 upper stage does the departure; your orbiter must keep its propellant for the capture, so every m/s the upper stage falls short comes out of the capture margin. After ten months of cruise a small midcourse correction a month out puts periapsis where you want it; then brake there.

campaign.title: Venus to Mercury
campaign.briefing: Reach Mercury slowly enough to matter: pass it below {pass} at under 13 km/s, after a flyby of Venus. Going straight to Mercury costs about the same to leave Earth but arrives near 16 km/s; Venus’s gravity bends the path for free. Launch in late 2031 on an Atlas V: the Centaur has the departure with a few per cent to spare, and your light probe has only about 500 m/s, so launch well.

campaign.title: Leave the Sun
campaign.briefing: Leave the solar system with at least 7.5 km/s of excess speed over the Sun. Even an Ariane 5 cannot do it alone: its upper stage gives about half the departure, then separates and your kick stage burns the rest in the same pass. Then fly behind Jupiter, so its gravity turns your path toward the direction Jupiter is moving and hands you some of its orbital speed. Launch in 2031 or 2032.

campaign.title: Jupiter to Saturn
campaign.briefing: Fly past Jupiter and on to Saturn (below {pass}) in under 7.4 years. The planets line up for this only about every 20 years; launch in 2034. The departure is split across a separation: the Ariane upper stage burns out, your kick stage finishes it. Aim the Jupiter flyby so it bends you toward where Saturn will be, and trim the path after the flyby with what the kick stage has left.
